title: WHY ONLY ONE MAN COULD ENTER THE MOST HOLY PLACE ONCE A YEAR
paragraphs:
WHY ONLY ONE MAN COULD ENTER THE MOST HOLY PLACE ONCE A YEAR
Behind that forbidden curtain was a terrifying message about your sin—and a breathtaking prophecy about the day Jesus would open the way home.
There was a room almost nobody on earth was allowed to enter.
Not the king.
Not the strongest warrior in Israel.
Not the wealthiest man.
Not the most respected elder.
Not even an ordinary priest.
One man.
One day.
Once a year.
And even he could not walk in casually.
He entered with blood.
Imagine standing outside that curtain.
You know what is behind it.
The ark of the covenant.
The place associated with the manifest presence of the Holy God.
The Most Holy Place.
And between you and that place hangs a veil that seems to preach without speaking:
You cannot simply walk into the presence of God on your own terms.
That sentence may feel uncomfortable in a generation accustomed to hearing that God should accept us however we choose to approach Him.
But Scripture does not begin the story of salvation by telling us how impressive humanity is.
It shows us how holy God is.
And how desperately we need mercy.
Leviticus 16 opens under the shadow of death.
“The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron who died when they approached the LORD.”
Nadab and Abihu had died after approaching God contrary to His command.
Then God spoke concerning Aaron.
The Hebrew warning of Leviticus 16:2 contains these words:
וְאַל־יָבֹא בְכָל־עֵת אֶל־הַקֹּדֶשׁ
Ve’al-yavo vekhol-et el-haqodesh.
In context:
He must not come “at every time” or whenever he wishes into the holy place.
Why?
Because the God on the other side of that curtain was not a religious accessory.
He was holy.
Utterly holy.
The problem was not that God was cruel.
The problem was that sinful humanity was attempting to stand before perfect holiness.
We sometimes speak about sin as though it were merely a collection of unfortunate mistakes.
God speaks about sin far more seriously.
Sin alienates.
Sin corrupts.
Sin enslaves.
Sin produces guilt.
Sin leads to death.
And perhaps one reason we struggle to understand the Gospel is that we have spent so much time making sin small that the cross no longer looks enormous.
If sin is merely a mistake, Jesus becomes merely an inspirational teacher.
But if sin has separated guilty human beings from a holy God, then suddenly Calvary becomes something breathtaking.
The Day of Atonement was preparing Israel to understand that.
Once each year, on Yom Kippur—the Day of Atonement—the high priest entered the Most Holy Place.
But before representing the people, the priest had a problem of his own.
He was sinful too.
Aaron could not stand before God and pretend he was different from everybody waiting outside.
He needed atonement himself.
That detail matters more than we sometimes realize.
The man representing sinners was himself a sinner.
The priest needed sacrifice.
The mediator needed mercy.
The one carrying blood for others needed blood offered for himself.
Hebrews later explains the scene with extraordinary precision:
εἰς δὲ τὴν δευτέραν ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ μόνος ὁ ἀρχιερεύς
The heart of the statement is unmistakable:
hapax tou eniautou—
“once in the year.”
Only the high priest entered the inner sanctuary, once each year, and not without blood.
Stop there.
Not without blood.
Because forgiveness is not God shrugging His shoulders at evil and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
It matters.
The lies mattered.
The lust mattered.
The hatred mattered.
The pride mattered.
The betrayal mattered.
The secret addiction mattered.
The cruelty nobody else saw mattered.
The words you wish you could pull back into your mouth mattered.
The nights when you knew exactly what God commanded and deliberately chose something else mattered.
Your sin matters.
Mine does too.
Yet this is where the story begins turning from terror toward grace.
Because the blood carried through that curtain was saying something.
Sin deserves judgment.
But God was providing a way of atonement.
The Hebrew language of Leviticus repeatedly uses the idea represented by כפר (k-p-r), commonly expressed in this context as “make atonement.”
The Day of Atonement was not humanity inventing a ladder high enough to reach God.
God Himself prescribed the way His covenant people were to approach.
The priest entered.
Atonement was made.
The people waited.
Then another year came.
And it happened again.
Another sacrifice.
Another Day of Atonement.
Another priest.
Another year.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Can you feel the incompleteness built into the repetition?
If the old sacrificial system had brought final perfection, why did the sacrifices continue?
Hebrews forces us to confront that question.
Those sacrifices pointed beyond themselves.
The earthly sanctuary was not the final destination.
The high priest was not the final Priest.
Animal blood was not the final sacrifice.
The curtain was not going to have the final word.
Someone greater was coming.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where the ancient ceremony suddenly reaches through thousands of years and grabs you personally.
Because Jesus did not arrive merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
The old high priest entered with blood belonging to another creature.
Jesus offered Himself.
The old high priest first needed sacrifice for his own sin.
Jesus was sinless.
The old high priest entered an earthly sanctuary.
Christ entered the greater reality to which the earthly sanctuary pointed.
The old priest's ministry had to be repeated.
Jesus offered the decisive sacrifice once for all.
Hebrews says Christ appeared “once for all” to deal with sin through His sacrifice.
Once.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Because His sacrifice was sufficient.
That changes everything.
You may have spent years believing God will finally receive you after you become clean enough.
So you hide.
You perform.
You promise.
You fail.
You cry.
You try again.
You delete the evidence.
You clean up your public image.
You learn Christian vocabulary.
You sit in church while carrying things inside you that nobody in the room knows.
People call you strong.
God knows you are exhausted.
People see your Sunday clothes.
God sees what happened Thursday night.
People hear your worship.
God hears the thoughts you never say aloud.
And somewhere underneath all that religious activity is a frightened question:
“If God really knew everything about me, would He still let me come near?”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not that God discovered your secrets and decided they were not serious.
The Gospel is that God knew the full horror of human sin and sent His Son anyway.
Jesus did not die for the edited version of you.
He died for sinners.
That is why repentance is not cleaning yourself before approaching Christ.
Repentance is turning from sin and coming to the Christ who alone can save you.
Grace does not tell you to keep loving what crucified your Savior.
Grace calls you out of darkness.
Grace forgives.
Grace cleanses.
Grace changes allegiance.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace takes people with histories they are ashamed to remember and gives them a future centered on Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps you need that sentence more than you want anyone to know.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody discovered the affair.
Nobody knows about the pornography.
Nobody knows how bitter you have become.
Nobody knows about the money.
Nobody knows about the secret messages.
Nobody knows how far your prayer life has collapsed.
Nobody knows that you can encourage everybody else while privately wondering whether God is tired of you.
But Jesus knows.
And remarkably, His invitation to repent is still standing.
Not an invitation to excuse your sin.
An invitation to leave it.
Not an invitation to pretend judgment is unreal.
An invitation to run to the One who bore judgment for sinners.
The ancient high priest walked behind the curtain carrying sacrificial blood.
Jesus walked toward a cross carrying Himself.
Think about that.
The hands that fashioned humanity were pierced by human hands.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
The spotless Lamb was sacrificed.
And when Christ died, the Gospel accounts tell us that the temple curtain was torn.
What generations had known as restricted access suddenly became an unforgettable sign.
But do not misunderstand it.
The torn veil does not mean holiness stopped mattering.
It means Jesus accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
We do not stroll into God's presence because we finally became worthy.
We draw near because Christ is worthy.
Hebrews therefore does something astonishing.
After explaining priesthood, sacrifice, blood, sanctuary and the once-for-all work of Jesus, it tells believers to draw near.
Draw near.
Those words should almost make you tremble after reading Leviticus.
Once, the warning was:
Do not come whenever you wish.
Now, because of Christ:
Draw near.
Once, one representative priest entered.
Now those who belong to Jesus have access to God through their great High Priest.
Once, sacrificial blood testified year after year that atonement was necessary.
Now the Church looks back to the finished sacrifice of the Lamb of God.
This is Christianity.
Not “be good enough and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
Not “follow your heart.”
Not “invent your own truth.”
Not “compare yourself with somebody worse and hope heaven grades on a curve.”
Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Our great High Priest.
Our only sufficient Savior.
Our righteousness is not enough.
His is.
Our payment is not enough.
His blood is.
Our religious performance cannot reconcile us to God.
Jesus can.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that you have committed too many sins to be saved.
It is that you could become so comfortable around Christian things that you never actually surrender yourself to Christ.
You can know worship songs and still hide.
You can repost Bible verses and still refuse repentance.
You can know church language and still love darkness.
You can defend Christianity online while Christ remains outside the locked rooms of your heart.
The high priest could not enter the Most Holy Place carrying confidence in himself.
Neither can you.
Come empty-handed.
Come guilty.
Come confessing.
Come believing.
Come because Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
There is grace for the person reading this with tears forming in their eyes.
There is grace for the prodigal.
Grace for the hypocrite who is finally tired of pretending.
Grace for the addict ready to drag the hidden chains into the light.
Grace for the husband who failed.
Grace for the wife carrying secret shame.
Grace for the believer whose faith has become cold.
Grace for the person who thinks, “After everything I've done, surely God doesn't want me anymore.”
Do not confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives also calls you to follow Him.
The Christ who receives sinners transforms sinners.
He does not merely rewrite where your story ends.
He begins rewriting who you are.
So repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding.
Bring the secret thing into His light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Make restitution where Scripture requires it and where it can rightly be made.
Seek help where you are enslaved.
Return to prayer.
Return to Scripture.
Return to fellowship.
But above everything else...
return to Jesus.
Maybe somebody you love needs to read this tonight.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Because you remember what it felt like when somebody cared enough to bring truth into your darkness.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know there is still mercy in Christ.
If you have been hiding from God, comment, “No more hiding.”
If your faith has been exhausted but you refuse to walk away from Jesus, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If conviction is breaking through something you have kept secret, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Somebody reading silently may need to see evidence that Christ still restores broken people.

And if you believe Gospel-centered truth like this should keep reaching believers, prodigals, seekers, struggling Christians, and people who may never voluntarily walk into a church, following and supporting Gospel Warrior is one practical way to help that mission continue.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
You cannot purchase grace.
Sharing an article cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus saves.
It is surrendering to Christ.
Because thousands of years ago, one man walked behind a curtain once a year carrying blood that could never be his final answer.
Then Jesus came.
And the temporary shadows gave way to the substance.
The repeated sacrifices pointed toward the sufficient sacrifice.
The sinful priests pointed toward the sinless High Priest.
The restricted sanctuary pointed toward access through Christ.
The blood pointed toward the Lamb.
And the curtain could not remain forever.
Maybe your whole life has felt like standing outside that curtain.
Too dirty.
Too ashamed.
Too far gone.
Too late.
But if you belong to Jesus, your hope is not that you finally became good enough to enter.
Your hope is that the perfect High Priest went before you.
So stop trying to save yourself.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is killing you.
Stop decorating the chains Christ is calling you to leave behind.
Turn around.
Look at the cross.
And come home.
The curtain said, “You cannot come this way alone.” The cross answered, “You don't have to—Jesus has made the way.”
